node.label: Canadian military history
node.period_rationale: Period 1 (c. 1945–70) is when official history dominates: Stanley 1954, Stacey 1955–70, Nicholson 1962. Duguid 1938 is an earlier root; war and society (Morton, Copp, Pierson) belongs to periods 2–3 and memory to period 3.
node.date_label: Duguid’s only official volume 1938 · Stacey’s official histories 1955–70 · Nicholson’s replacement CEF history 1962 · Broken Promises 1977 · war-and-society studies 1986–93 · Walker on race and recruitment 1989 · Valour and the Horror broadcast and hearings 1992 · Vance 1997 · coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones and one public controversy (broadcast January 1992, Senate hearings and Ombudsman’s report later that year; documented in a 1994 volume). 1938 is an earlier official history, not the field’s origin; 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

node.description: Canadian military history has three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. Early work was largely official history, published by authority of the Minister of National Defence. Duguid’s official history of the Great War produced only one volume (1938); Nicholson’s Canadian Expeditionary Force (1962) replaced it. Stacey wrote volumes I (1955) and III (1960) of the Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, and his Arms, Men and Governments (1970) made war policy a subject; Stanley’s Canada’s Soldiers (1954) called Canadians ‘an unmilitary people’. Conscription and French-Canadian participation recur, from Armstrong’s Crisis of Quebec (1937) to Granatstein and Hitsman’s Broken Promises (1977) and francophone histories of the 22nd Battalion (Gagnon 1986) and of bilingualism in the forces (Pariseau and Bernier 1987). From the 1980s war-and-society history turned to soldiers, veterans, psychiatry and women: Morton’s military and political histories (1981, 1985), veterans’ return (Morton and Wright 1987), battle exhaustion (Copp and McAndrew 1990) and Pierson on wartime womanhood (1986). Walker (1989) studied the enlistment of visible minorities, and Dempsey Prairie First Nations soldiers (1999). Popular history (Berton’s Vimy, 1986) and the CBC series The Valour and the Horror (1992), which led to Senate hearings and an ombudsman’s report, made military history a major public controversy. Vance’s Death So Noble (1997) treated the Great War as a cultural force in interwar memory. Cook (2002, 2006) showed that the records and narratives of Stacey’s officers were neither neutral nor unbiased.
node.scope_note: A research field with three overlapping modes: official and operational history, war and society, and memory and public history. They are not successive stages; official historians also wrote policy history, and war-and-society historians also wrote operations. Popular history (Berton) and public controversy are included as part of the field’s public life, not as academic scholarship. Francophone work on conscription and French-Canadian participation is part of the field and meets Quebec historiography. Several roster people have primary placements elsewhere (Stanley, Granatstein, Copp, Bercuson, Pierson, Vance); they appear for specific works. Imperial, naval and air histories and the Royal Military College tradition are thin in this selection. Critics of militarized memory (McKay and Swift) are after 2000. Black and Japanese-Canadian soldiers appear through Walker (1989, scholarly) and two community and veteran histories (Ruck 1987, Ito 1984). The Valour and the Horror controversy is a strand here, called a major public-history controversy on a contemporary witness (Dick 1993); Carr’s later treatment (CHR 2005) is unread, so it is not called a defining historiographical controversy.

strands.title: Official history
strands.focus: Duguid’s interwar official history (1938, the only volume published; Gustavson 2001), Stacey’s volumes I and III of the Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War (1955, 1960) and Nicholson’s CEF (1962), which replaced Duguid’s series. Cook (2002, 2006) shows the historical officers making the records and the narrative later historians used, from sources neither neutral nor unbiased.

strands.title: National military history and war policy
strands.focus: Stanley’s ‘unmilitary people’ (1954), Stacey’s war policies (1970) and Morton’s military and political histories (1981, 1985).

strands.title: Conscription and French Canada
strands.focus: Armstrong’s interwar study of Quebec’s crisis (1937), Granatstein and Hitsman’s conscription history (1977), and francophone histories from the Laval press and the defence historical service (Gagnon 1986; Pariseau and Bernier 1987). Gagnon’s 1995 essay assesses how French-Canadian historians wrote about the Second World War, in a dossier on ‘myths and realities’.
strands.works: Armstrong (1937); Granatstein and Hitsman (1977); Gagnon (1986, 1995); Pariseau and Bernier (1987)

strands.title: War and society: soldiers, veterans, psychiatry, women
strands.focus: Veterans’ return (Morton and Wright 1987), the ordinary soldier (Morton 1993), battle exhaustion and psychiatry (Copp and McAndrew 1990) and women and Canadian womanhood (Pierson 1986).
strands.works: Pierson (1986); Morton and Wright (1987); Copp and McAndrew (1990); Morton (1993)

strands.title: Visible minorities and Indigenous soldiers
strands.focus: Walker’s study of the enlistment of visible minorities in the CEF (1989) is the checked pre-2000 scholarly history; Ruck (1987) on the Black No. 2 Construction Battalion and Ito (1984) on Japanese-Canadian soldiers are community and veteran histories by non-academic authors; Dempsey (1999) studies Prairie First Nations soldiers. Title and catalogue level only.

strands.title: The home front, propaganda and community
strands.focus: Propaganda and censorship in the Great War (Keshen 1996), and after 2000 the Second World War home front (Keshen 2004) and local responses to the Great War (Rutherdale 2004).

strands.title: Memory and myth
strands.focus: Vance treats the Great War as a cultural and philosophical force in interwar memory (1997); Cook’s history of the writing of the world wars (2006) extends the question to historians themselves.

strands.title: Popular history and public controversy
strands.focus: Berton’s Vimy (1986) as popular history; the CBC series The Valour and the Horror (aired January 1992), which led to Senate subcommittee hearings from late June 1992 and a CBC Ombudsman’s report released on 10 November 1992. Dick (1993) called the reaction unprecedented; Bercuson and Wise (1994) collect the reports for the Ombudsman, the Ombudsman’s report, the McKennas’ reply and new essays. A major public-history controversy; Carr’s later historiographical treatment (2005) is unread. McKay and Swift’s Warrior Nation (2012, extension, title-level) criticizes a later militarized national memory.
strands.works: Berton (1986); Dick (1993); Bercuson and Wise, eds. (1994); McKay and Swift (2012)

extension_coverage.note: Selected post-2000 works only. Tim Cook’s operational histories, the centenary literature, and newer work on Indigenous, Black and Asian Canadian soldiers are not reviewed.

relation_to_periods: Main-period entry with official history in period 1, war and society in periods 2–3 and memory in period 3. Post-2000 selections (Cook 2002, 2006; Keshen 2004; Rutherdale 2004; McKay and Swift 2012) are extension records.

proposed_relationships.relationship: A national field within military history
proposed_relationships.map_label: Canadian military history and military history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The atlas’s Military history entry has no Canadian participants. Cook’s account of Stacey and the Army Historical Section (official history as archive-making and narrative) parallels the military entry’s concern with source access and narrative framing. Comparison: the Canadian field is not presented as derived from Howard or Keegan.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Great War memory in interwar Canada
proposed_relationships.map_label: Vance: memory of the Great War
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Vance’s Death So Noble examines Canada’s collective memory of the Great War in the 1920s and 1930s as a cultural and philosophical force (publisher description). A contribution to the memory entry’s war_mourning strand alongside Winter; no claim that Vance derives from Winter. Cook (2006) extends the question to historians’ own role. PhD context: Death So Noble is cited by 67 PhDs 2009–2026, the most of any work by this roster.

Armstrong (1937), Granatstein and Hitsman (1977), Gagnon (1986, 1995) and Pariseau (1987) write conscription and French-Canadian participation; Gagnon’s 1995 essay assesses French-Canadian historians’ treatment of the Second World War in a Bulletin d’histoire politique dossier on ‘myths and realities’. Overlapping subject and venues, different questions. PhD context: 53 PhDs engage both rosters (expected 26.9).

proposed_relationships.map_label: Women and the Second World War
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Pierson’s “They’re Still Women After All”: The Second World War and Canadian Womanhood (1986) belongs to both fields; Pierson anchors the proposed women and gender entry. Title-level.

The CBC series The Valour and the Horror aired in January 1992; Senate subcommittee hearings began in late June 1992 and the CBC Ombudsman’s report was released on 10 November 1992. Dick (Archivaria, 1993) says the series ‘prompted unprecedented public reaction and discussion’. Official and academic historians wrote reports for the Ombudsman, collected with an appendix on the RCAF official history in Bercuson and Wise (1994; contents checked). Berton’s popular Vimy (1986) is a second witness. Comparison with the Public history entry; no direction asserted.

Stacey’s Arms, Men and Governments: The War Policies of Canada (1970) and Morton’s Canada and War: A Military and Political History (1981) join military to political history; Granatstein anchors both entries. Title-level; the political-history drafter may hold stronger sources.
proposed_relationships.merge_note: Same pair and kind as cdng_pn_rel_04 in the cdn_political_national draft (Stacey 1970, Granatstein 1975, Granatstein and Hitsman 1977). Accept one edge carrying both source sets.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: No checked source links Canadian official historians to the strategic-scholarship tradition (Clausewitz, Delbrück) or to staff-college teaching.

Overlap is high (150 PhDs; 86, lift 2.69, with the shared people Copp, Bercuson and Morton removed), but no checked source links the fields. A lead: veterans, welfare and soldiers’ families (Morton) are where they meet.
Dempsey (1999) on Prairie First Nations soldiers is a lead, title-level only; Stanley is on both rosters. Now in the strand on visible minorities and Indigenous soldiers.
Granatstein links them; left to the who_killed_debate drafter.
McKay and Swift’s Warrior Nation (2012) is a critique of militarized memory, title-level and post-2000; Vance’s primary placement is cdn_intellectual_cultural. Leads, not proposals.

open_questions: Label: groups.json’s long label (“official history, war & society, memory”) is used. A shorter “Canadian military history” with the three modes in the description would match the atlas’s other labels better.
Pariseau (1987) is cited under Pariseau alone, as in the catalogue. Is Serge Bernier a coauthor of the 1987 volume? Not verified here.
Stacey 1955 and 1960: the series title (official history of the Canadian Army in the Second World War) is not in the catalogue records and is not cited; confirm for the release.
Duguid: did only one volume of the interwar official history appear? Cook’s Clio’s Warriors would settle it; not read here.
Berton is a ‘contributor’ (popular historian). Keep him on the roster, as groups.json does, or move him to a strand?
The Valour and the Horror controversy is a candidate debate in its own right. Keep it as a strand here?
Indigenous, Black and Asian Canadian soldiers are represented only by Dempsey (1999). Add a pre-2000 Black or Japanese-Canadian military history if one is checked?

question_resolutions.summary: Label shortened to 'Canadian military history'; the description opens with the three overlapping modes (official and operational history, war and society, memory and public history).

Serge Bernier added as coauthor with the subtitle and series (tome 1, 1763–1969: le spectre d’une armée bicéphale, 1987), checked against the DND official-histories page and a BHP review header; Bernier added as strand credit.
Stacey 1955 and 1960 now cite the series Official History of the Canadian Army in the Second World War, vol. I and vol. III, checked against the DND page and the official-histories list.
Duguid's 1938 volume is described as the only volume published, with Nicholson 1962 as its replacement; Gustavson (CMH 2001, abstract read) added as the source.
Berton stays on the roster as a popular-history contributor (54 citing PhDs).

Kept as a strand with the checked 1992 dates (broadcast, Senate hearings, Ombudsman's report) and the 1994 volume; called a major public-history controversy citing Dick (Archivaria 1993, new source). Not called 'defining': Carr 2005 is unread.
Walker (CHR 1989) added as the scholarly anchor and roster row; Ruck (1987) and Ito (1984) added as community and veteran histories in a new strand with Dempsey.
